books.section: Topic 4.11 An Age of Reform, A. Reform Movements in the Antebellum Period

stimulus.text: This view of Lowell, Massachusetts, published between 1840 and 1860, shows a row of large brick textile mills along the Merrimack River, with church steeples and houses behind them and farm fields in the foreground.
stimulus.source_note: View of Lowell, Massachusetts, 1840-1860, Library of Congress (LCCN94515606), public domain. Image viewed before writing.

source: original; stimulus image from the shared pool, View of Lowell, 1840-1860, public domain
stem: The mills in the image best illustrate which change of the Market Revolution?

options.text: Farming replaced factory work across New England
options.misconception: The image shows factories rising, not farms replacing them.

options.text: Trade with Europe came to a sudden end
options.misconception: Lowell sold cloth in American markets and bought Southern cotton; trade continued.

options.text: Slavery expanded across New England towns
options.misconception: Slavery had been outlawed in New England; Lowell's workers were free wage laborers.

options.text: Production moved from homes into factories using wage labor

rationales.A: The mills are the change, not farming. Workers left farms to tend power looms in factories.
rationales.B: Lowell's cloth competed in American markets, and its cotton came from the South. Trade did not end; it grew.
rationales.C: Massachusetts had ended slavery in the 1780s. Lowell's mill workers were young farm women earning wages.
rationales.D: Before the mills, cloth was made at home. The image shows production gathered into huge factories, run by wage workers.
rationales.general:
1. Compare the old way. Cloth was once woven at home, by hand.
2. Look at the new way. The image shows rows of mills, each holding hundreds of looms.
3. Name the workers. Young women earned cash wages tending the machines.
Background: The Lowell system hired farm daughters and housed them in company boardinghouses.
Remember: a factory in a picture is a before-and-after — ask what the work looked like before the building.
